summary: Chinese has one small set of personal pronouns that never change: 我 wǒ ‘I, me’, 你 nǐ ‘you’ (polite 您 nín), 他 / 她 / 它 tā ‘he, she, it’. The plural adds 们 men: 我们 ‘we’, 你们 ‘you (all)’, 他们 / 她们 / 它们 ‘they’; 咱们 is ‘we’ including the listener. The same form is subject and object, and the verb does not change with the person: 我是, 你是, 他们是.

head: Singular
Plural (+ 们)
rows: 我们 wǒmen — we, us; 咱们 zánmen — we (you and I)
你 nǐ — you; 您 nín — you (polite)
他 tā — he; 她 tā — she; 它 tā — it
他们 — they (men or mixed); 她们 — they (women); 它们 — they (things, animals)
blocks.caption: The personal pronouns

blocks.title: One form for every job
blocks.text: 我 is ‘I’ and ‘me’: 我是学生 ‘I am a student’ — 他喜欢我 ‘he likes me’. ‘My’ is 我的 (lesson S06).

blocks.title: tā is one sound
blocks.text: 他, 她 and 它 are all pronounced tā; a mixed group is 他们, even with one man among many women.

items.title: 我们 wǒmen
points: may exclude the listener: 我们走了，你呢？ ‘we’re going — and you?’

blocks.title: 您 and the plural
blocks.text: There is no standard polite plural *您们: to a group say 你们, or politely 各位 / 大家.

askYourself: Who is the subject — me, the listener, someone else? Pick 我, 你 / 您, 他 / 她 / 它.
Is the listener older, a teacher, a customer or a stranger to be respected? → 您.
More than one person? → add 们: 我们, 你们, 他们 — or 咱们 if the listener is included.
A group of only women? → 她们; any man in it → 他们; things or animals → 它们 (often left out).
Is the verb changing? → never: 我是, 他们是.
steps: Choose the pronoun by person, respect and number.
Use the same form as an object: 老师认识我.

traps: *我们们 or *您们 — 们 only once, and not on 您.
Using 您 with close friends sounds cold or ironic.
咱们 must include the listener: never *咱们走了，你呢？
它 is much rarer than English ‘it’: no dummy subject (是我 ‘it’s me’).

quiz.why: 您 is the polite ‘you’ for teachers, elders and customers.

quiz.q: ‘They’ for two girls and one boy?
quiz.why: As soon as one man is in the group, the plural is 他们.
我 is also the object form — no change.

quiz.q: How do 他 and 她 sound?
quiz.why: The difference exists only in writing.

seeAlso.note: German du / Sie match 你 / 您, but German pronouns change with case (ich – mich – mir) and the verb agrees (ich bin, du bist).
Arabic has gender in ‘you’ (anta / anti) and a dual (antumā); Chinese has one 你 and no dual.
Hebrew has a masculine and a feminine ‘you’ (atá / at) and ‘they’ (hem / hen); Chinese marks gender only in writing (他们 / 她们).
